interfaces.name: Matrix factor model
interfaces.type_shape: Matrix-valued factor model with distinct positive, one-way and zero-factor conventions. The one-way cases are not obtained by silently multiplying empty factor matrices in (1.1). Assumptions B1-B4 are supplementary and unresolved.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Matrix-valued factor model with distinct positive, one-way and zero-factor conventions. The one-way cases are not obtained by silently multiplying empty factor matrices in (1.1). Assumptions B1-B4 are supplementary and unresolved.

members.local_label: Section 1 — matrix factor model and zero-factor conventions (1.1)–(1.2)
members.source_heading: Section 1 — matrix factor model and zero-factor conventions (1.1)–(1.2)
members.statement_original:
To fix ideas, let $\{X_t,t=1,2,...\}$ be a time series of $p_1\times p_2$ matrices. A matrix factor model with common factors can be written as
\[
(X_t)_{p_1\times p_2}=(R)_{p_1\times k_1}(F_t)_{k_1\times k_2}(C')_{k_2\times p_2}+(E_t)_{p_1\times p_2},\quad k_1,k_2>0,\tag{1.1}
\]
where the subscripts represent the row and column dimensions of each matrix. In (1.1), $R$ is a $p_1\times k_1$ matrix of loadings explaining the variations of $X_t$ across the rows, $C$ is a $p_2\times k_2$ matrix of loadings reflecting the differences across the columns of $X_t$, $F_t$ is a matrix of common factors, and $E_t$ is the idiosyncratic component, and we assume that factor numbers $k_1$ and $k_2$ are positive, demonstrating a collaborative dependence between both the cross-row and the cross-column dimensions. The matrix factor structure in (1.1) is also known as a two-way factor structure, and we use the same convention as in He et al. (2021) that
\[
(X_t)_{p_1\times p_2}=
\begin{cases}
(R)_{p_1\times k_1}(F_t)_{k_1\times p_2}+(E_t)_{p_1\times p_2},&k_1>0,\ k_2=0,\\
(F_t)_{p_1\times k_2}(C')_{k_2\times p_2}+(E_t)_{p_1\times p_2},&k_2>0,\ k_1=0,\\
(E_t)_{p_1\times p_2},&k_1=k_2=0,
\end{cases}\tag{1.2}
\]
to indicate that there may be no column common factors (first case), no row common factors (second case) or no factor structure at all (third case).

interfaces.type_shape: Uncentered projected second moment with window length m. Preserve the printed full-T initial covariance and row-product order; the source does not specify a causal estimator update or eigenvector tie convention here.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Uncentered projected second moment with window length m. Preserve the printed full-T initial covariance and row-product order; the source does not specify a causal estimator update or eigenvector tie convention here.

members.local_label: Section 2 — projected covariance and initial projection estimator
members.source_heading: Section 2 — projected covariance and initial projection estimator
members.statement_original:
In order to fully make use of the two-way interactive factor structure, we propose studying the spectrum of a projected column (row) covariance matrix, as suggested by Yu et al. (2021). Heuristically, if $C$ is known and satisfies the orthogonality condition $C'C/p_2=I_{k_2}$, the data matrix can be projected into a lower dimensional space by setting $Y_t=X_tC/p_2$. In view of this, we define
\[
\widehat M_1=\frac1m\sum_{t=1}^m\widetilde Y_t\widetilde Y_t',\tag{2.4}
\]
where $\widetilde Y_t=p_2^{-1}X_t\widetilde C$ and $\widetilde C$ is an initial estimator of $C$. As suggested by Yu et al. (2021), the initial estimator can be set as $\widetilde C=\sqrt{p_2}Q$, where the columns of $Q$ are the leading $k_2$ eigenvectors of $M_r$, where $M_r$ is the column “flattened” sample covariance matrices, i.e.,
\[
M_r:=\frac1{Tp_1}\sum_{t=1}^T X_t'X_t=\frac1{Tp_1}\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{j=1}^{p_1}X_{j\cdot,t}X_{j\cdot,t}'.
\]
Furthermore, if $k_2$ is not known, we can select the leading $\widetilde k$ eigenvectors of $M_r$ with $\widetilde k$ chosen such that $\widetilde k\ge k_2$ (we refer to Section 5 for details on how we choose $\widetilde k$).

interfaces.name: Eigenvalue
interfaces.type_shape: The (k1+1)-th eigenvalue in decreasing order, computed on observations tau+1,...,m+tau. Monitoring time tau is relative to the training length m; T=m+Tm.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: The (k1+1)-th eigenvalue in decreasing order, computed on observations tau+1,...,m+tau. Monitoring time tau is relative to the training length m; T=m+Tm.

members.statement_original:
We monitor for changepoints in the row factor structure of $X_t$ across an interval $m+1\le t\le m+T_m$, with - tidying up the notation - $m+T_m=T$. The monitoring schemes are based on the eigenvalue
\[
\widehat\lambda_{k_1+1,\tau}=\lambda_{k_1+1}\left(\frac1m\sum_{t=\tau+1}^{m+\tau}\widetilde Y_t\widetilde Y_t^\top\right),
\]
where $\widetilde Y_t=p_2^{-1}X_t\widetilde C$.

interfaces.name: Sequence
interfaces.type_shape: Deterministic rate sequence. The square root covers m times p2, and the exponent 1+epsilon applies to the whole logarithmic product. This epsilon is the arbitrarily positive rate slack, not automatically the tuning epsilon in (3.14).
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Deterministic rate sequence. The square root covers m times p2, and the exponent 1+epsilon applies to the whole logarithmic product. This epsilon is the arbitrarily positive rate slack, not automatically the tuning epsilon in (3.14).

members.statement_original:
Throughout the paper, we often use the following sequence
\[
l_{p_1,p_2,m}=\left(\frac1{p_2}+\frac1m+\frac{p_1}{\sqrt{mp_2}}\right)\left(\ln^2p_1\ln p_2\ln m\right)^{1+\epsilon}.\tag{1.3}
\]

interfaces.name: Column space
interfaces.type_shape: No change of the row-factor loading space during training. Theorem 3 does not explicitly list C1, although it appears in the section setup.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: No change of the row-factor loading space during training. Theorem 3 does not explicitly list C1, although it appears in the section setup.

members.statement_original: The column space of $R$ does not change during $1\le t\le m$.

interfaces.name: Monitoring
interfaces.type_shape: Diverging monitoring horizon with at least the stated polynomial lower growth. Keep ordinary Omega here distinct from the explicitly defined almost-sure Omega convention.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Diverging monitoring horizon with at least the stated polynomial lower growth. Keep ordinary Omega here distinct from the explicitly defined almost-sure Omega convention.

members.statement_original: It holds that $T_m=T_m(m)$ with $\lim_{m\to\infty}T_m=\infty$, and $T_m=\Omega(m^\varsigma)$ with $\varsigma\ge1$.

naming_context.text: We allow the monitoring $T_m$ to go on for a long time.

interfaces.name: Row factor space
interfaces.type_shape: Fixed number of row factors with a changed loading space. The break is at calendar time m+t*, not t* alone. No orthogonality or rank conditions from supplementary B assumptions are invented.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Fixed number of row factors with a changed loading space. The break is at calendar time m+t*, not t* alone. No orthogonality or rank conditions from supplementary B assumptions are invented.

members.statement_original:
A first source of change could be a scenario in which the number of common factors is constant across regimes, but the row factor space spanned by the columns of $R$ switches from one to another after a point in time $t^*$, i.e.,
\[
X_t=
\begin{cases}
RF_{1,t}C'+E_t&\text{for }1\le t\le m+t^*,\\
\widetilde R F_{2,t}C'+E_t&\text{for }t>m+t^*,
\end{cases}\tag{3.7}
\]
where $R=[R_0|R_1]$, $\widetilde R=[R_0|R_2]$, $R_0$ is a $p_1\times(k_1-c_1)$ matrix of loadings which do not undergo a change, and $R_1$ and $R_2$ are $p_1\times c_1$ matrices of loadings which differ before and after the changepoint $t^*$. We would like to point out that, in (3.7) and henceforth, we assume that $C$ does not change merely for simplicity.

interfaces.name: Common factors
interfaces.type_shape: Additional row factors after calendar time m+t*. This differs from the fixed-count space-change alternative. The unchanged column loading is the section convention; later extensions are not imported.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Additional row factors after calendar time m+t*. This differs from the fixed-count space-change alternative. The unchanged column loading is the section convention; later extensions are not imported.

members.statement_original:
As a second possible alternative, we consider the scenario whereby a set of common factors appear after the point in time $t^*$, i.e., the column space of $R$ enlarges:
\[
X_t=
\begin{cases}
RF_{a,t}C'+E_t&\text{for }1\le t\le m+t^*,\\
\widetilde R F_tC'+E_t&\text{for }t>m+t^*,
\end{cases}\tag{3.9}
\]
where $\widetilde R=[R|R_3]$, $R_3$ is a $p_1\times c_3$ matrix, $F_t'=[F_{a,t}'|F_{b,t}']$, and $F_{b,t}$ is a $c_3\times k_2$ matrix of new common factors.

interfaces.name: Continuous transformation
interfaces.type_shape: Original passage defines the transformation and its application to the normalized eigenvalue. The denominator is the trace divided by p1. Delta is the separately archived source tuning rule; no unspecified zero-trace convention or monotonicity assumption is added.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original passage defines the transformation and its application to the normalized eigenvalue. The denominator is the trace divided by p1. Delta is the separately archived source tuning rule; no unspecified zero-trace convention or monotonicity assumption is added.

members.local_label: Section 3 — continuous transformation and normalized sequence (3.15)
members.source_heading: Section 3 — continuous transformation and normalized sequence (3.15)
members.statement_original:
The dichotomous behaviour in (3.13) is the building block of our monitoring schemes, and it can be further enhanced by considering a continuous transformation $g(\cdot)$ such that $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty}g(x)=\infty$. Defining
\[
\psi_\tau=g\left(\frac{p_1^{-\delta}\widehat\lambda_{k_1+1,\tau}}{p_1^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{p_1}\widehat\lambda_{j,\tau}}\right),\tag{3.15}
\]
where $\widehat\lambda_{k_1+1,\tau}$ is normalised by the trace of $\left(\frac1m\sum_{t=\tau+1}^{m+\tau}\widetilde Y_t\widetilde Y_t^\top\right)$; again, other rescaling schemes are possible.

interfaces.name: New sequence
interfaces.type_shape: Gaussian randomization around the data-dependent drift. The null drift vanishes asymptotically; y_tau is not exactly centered iid normal at finite sample. The conditional construction is preserved without silently asserting an unstated sampling protocol.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Gaussian randomization around the data-dependent drift. The null drift vanishes asymptotically; y_tau is not exactly centered iid normal at finite sample. The conditional construction is preserved without silently asserting an unstated sampling protocol.

members.statement_original:
Finally, after computing $\psi_\tau$ at each $1\le\tau\le T_m$, we define the new sequence $\{y_\tau,1\le\tau\le T_m\}$ as
\[
y_\tau=z_\tau+\psi_\tau,\tag{3.16}
\]
where $z_\tau\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}N(0,1)$ for $1\le\tau\le T_m$.

interfaces.name: Functional form
interfaces.type_shape: Uniform monitoring-horizon control of the null drift scale. The printed limit uses min(p1,Tm), unlike the min(m,p1,p2) theorem limits. Delta is resolved by the auxiliary original tuning passage.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Uniform monitoring-horizon control of the null drift scale. The printed limit uses min(p1,Tm), unlike the min(m,p1,p2) theorem limits. Delta is resolved by the auxiliary original tuning passage.

members.statement_original:
In both cases, we will need the following restriction on the functional form of $g(\cdot)$:
\[
\lim_{\min(p_1,T_m)\to\infty}T_mg\left(p_1^{-\delta}l_{p_1,p_2,m}\right)=0.\tag{3.17}
\]

interfaces.name: Probability conditional
interfaces.type_shape: Conditional inference given the original observations, with almost-all-data-realizations qualification in every theorem. Do not replace conditional probability by the original data law.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Conditional inference given the original observations, with almost-all-data-realizations qualification in every theorem. Do not replace conditional probability by the original data law.

members.statement_original: Henceforth, we let $P^*$ denote the probability conditional on $\{X_t,1\le t\le T\}$; we use “$\xrightarrow{P^*}$”, and “$\xrightarrow{D^*}$” to denote convergence in probability and in distribution according to $P^*$, respectively.

interfaces.name: Partial sums process
interfaces.type_shape: Uncentered partial sum of the randomized sequence; not a Brownian bridge or a demeaned CUSUM.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Uncentered partial sum of the randomized sequence; not a Brownian bridge or a demeaned CUSUM.

members.statement_original:
In particular, recall the definition of $y_\tau$ in (3.16), and consider the partial sums process
\[
S_\tau=\sum_{j=1}^\tau y_j.\tag{3.18}
\]

interfaces.name: Weighted functionals
interfaces.type_shape: Monitoring-normalized maximum for eta strictly below one half. Eta=one half and trimmed eta-above-one-half regimes are separate source definitions.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Monitoring-normalized maximum for eta strictly below one half. Eta=one half and trimmed eta-above-one-half regimes are separate source definitions.

interfaces.name: Standardised partial sums
interfaces.type_shape: Borderline eta=one-half maximum. The separate alpha_Tm and beta_Tm normalizers are archived as an auxiliary original passage.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Borderline eta=one-half maximum. The separate alpha_Tm and beta_Tm normalizers are archived as an auxiliary original passage.

interfaces.name: Rényi statistics
interfaces.type_shape: Eta greater than one half with a diverging but negligible fraction of initial monitoring times omitted. The normalization is r_Tm^(eta-1/2), not Tm^(eta-1/2).
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Eta greater than one half with a diverging but negligible fraction of initial monitoring times omitted. The normalization is r_Tm^(eta-1/2), not Tm^(eta-1/2).

members.statement_original:
(iii) the Rényi statistics (see Horváth et al., 2020)
\[
r_{T_m}^{\eta-1/2}\max_{r_{T_m}\le\tau\le T_m}\frac{|S_\tau|}{\tau^\eta},\tag{3.21}
\]
for $\eta>1/2$, where $r_{T_m}$ is a sequence such that, as $T_m\to\infty$,
\[
r_{T_m}\to\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{r_{T_m}}{T_m}\to0.
\]

interfaces.name: Worst-case scenario
interfaces.type_shape: One-sided maximum without absolute values. The surrounding iid-Gaussian description is heuristic under the null; the actual observations contain the data-dependent drift.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: One-sided maximum without absolute values. The surrounding iid-Gaussian description is heuristic under the null; the actual observations contain the data-dependent drift.

members.statement_original:
These features (independence and Gaussianity) allow to propose a completely different monitoring scheme based on
\[
Z_{T_m}=\max_{1\le\tau\le T_m}y_\tau.\tag{3.31}
\]

naming_context.text: Monitoring schemes based on worst-case scenario

interfaces.name: Norming sequences
interfaces.type_shape: Centering b and scale a for the raw maximum statistic. They differ from the iterated-log alpha,beta normalization for standardized partial sums. Expressions are interpreted for sufficiently large Tm.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Centering b and scale a for the raw maximum statistic. They differ from the iterated-log alpha,beta normalization for standardized partial sums. Expressions are interpreted for sufficiently large Tm.

members.statement_original:
In order to study the asymptotics of $Z_{T_m}$, we define the norming sequences
\[
a_{T_m}=\frac{b_{T_m}}{1+b_{T_m}^2},\qquad b_{T_m}=\sqrt{2\ln T_m}-\frac{\ln\ln T_m+\ln(4\pi)}{2\sqrt{2\ln T_m}},
\]
which are proposed in Gasull et al. (2015).
